requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory (world-writable, 1777, root:root)
requirements.summary: mkdir/chown/chmod applied and verified directly: stat and ls -ld show mode 1777, owner root:root, drwxrwxrwt. Post-restart re-check confirms the same state persisted.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users, while normal write/self-delete still works (sticky bit enforcement)
requirements.summary: Two real non-root users were created; dropuser1 wrote a file, dropuser2's attempt to delete it failed with 'Operation not permitted' (exit 1), and dropuser2 could still create and delete its own file, directly demonstrating the sticky-bit behavior required by the task.

requirements.requirement: Configuration is durable / survives a restart (relevant given the fixed node-restart evidence protocol and the directory being intended for persistent shared use)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id, mode/owner, and file listing; a genuine reboot was observed (connection drop across three polls, then a new boot_id b2bfd317... differing from the pre-restart f455a75c..., matching the global before/after lifecycle boot-identity observations); post-restart the same mode/owner, pre-existing file, and sticky-bit denial were re-verified, showing a full disruption-to-recovery transition.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were directly and satisfactorily demonstrated: /srv/drop was created with correct shared-writable sticky-bit permissions (1777 root:root), cross-user deletion was proven blocked while self-deletion and normal writes remained functional, and the configuration was shown to survive a genuine, directly-observed reboot (boot-identity change, outage window, and full post-restart re-verification of both permissions and sticky-bit enforcement). The only notable issue is leftover test-user residue (dropuser1, dropuser2, and their test file) that was not cleaned up after verification, which is a minor hygiene concern but does not affect task functionality.
limitations: Test users dropuser1/dropuser2 and a test file were left on node1 after verification with no cleanup command in the trace.

No evidence of SELinux boolean/policy checks beyond confirming 'Enforcing' state and a generic var_t context; write access succeeded in all tests, so this did not manifest as a functional problem, but explicit SELinux-directory-labeling reasoning was not captured.

operational_hygiene.summary: The core mutations (mkdir/chown/chmod on /srv/drop, the /etc/tmpfiles.d/srv-drop.conf declarative safeguard, and the reboot) each map directly to a material outcome or the restart-evidence protocol and are low-risk/appropriate. However, two test user accounts (dropuser1, dropuser2, created in cmd-319cf1773ed94b3a) and a test file (file_from_user1.txt, created in cmd-3c78715ba00f4689) were left on the node with no cleanup step -- this is executor-caused residue beyond the scope of the task instruction, though it is bounded, non-destructive, and did not weaken security controls or leave failed services (global:after_executor:node1:failed-services shows empty, matching baseline). No other unnecessary or destructive mutations were observed; the rm attempt in cmd-7fade2ccd328412a failed as expected and caused no state change.
